#8376. Jost Kobusch to Train For Everest on Difficult, Dangerous Lhotse Shar

Jost Kobusch of Germany has moved to the Khumbu Valley to finish his acclimatization before attempting to solo winter Everest, beginning on December 22. His preparations include reaching 8,000m on a different peak.

Kobusch is now in Chukhung village, from which he climbed 6,165m Island Peak (Imja Tse) yesterday. He spent the night at 6,000m, topped out again today, and went back down, as shown in his live tracker. He told ExplorersWeb that he will now rest for a few days in Lukla and then hike up the valley again to inspect conditions on his next acclimatization goal: the difficult Lhotse Shar (8,383m).

Kobusch’s climb on Island Peak as shown in his tracker today.

“My plan is not to summit but to tag 8,000m up its flank, before heading for Everest,” he said.

Lhotse Shar is one of the main points of the Lhotse ridge, and it is climbed from south side of the mountain, with Chukhung as the starting point. The main options are to climb the southeastern flank of the Shar itself or try a direct line up the formidable south face of Lhotse.

Neither of them is easy, and the upper sections are statistically dangerous. According to Wikipedia, Lhotse Shar has the highest fatality rate of all principal or secondary 8,000m peaks. For every two climbers who summit, one person dies attempting to.

Lhotse and its various points, as seen from the south. Graphic by Gorskie Mapy

The Austrian expedition that first reached the summit of Lhotse Shar (from the Southeast Ridge) in 1970 set four altitude camps, the uppermost at 7,600m. They used supplemental oxygen on their summit push. “Almost the whole of the route from below Camp 1 to Camp 3 was fixed with rope, as climbing was very difficult,” they reported in the AAJ.

Kobusch will not have to deal with the nearly vertical terrain and cornices near the summit, but will have to face difficult mixed terrain and uncertain conditions if he wants to venture up to 8,000m. He will not use bottled oxygen, and as far as we know, he will climb on his own.

Kobusch plans to reach the base of Everest on December 22 and solo the mountain in winter without oxygen, via the West Ridge — the same line currently being attempted by a Russian team.

This is Kobusch’s fourth attempt, and he is willing to try to reach the summit this time. However, when asked about it, he admits he does not know if such a feat is actually possible. “Every expedition, every training session, every difficult decision has been part of preparing myself for what I know will be the biggest challenge of my life,” he admits.

Kobusch’s is not the only confirmed climb this winter. Denis Urubko of Russia is reportedly preparing to climb Broad Peak in winter, possibly starting at the end of this year and continuing through January and February. On social media, Urubko mentioned he will be climbing with Vitaliy Skel. However, details of his route have not been confirmed.

Simone Moro of Italy has not decided whether to try Manaslu again this winter. He told ExplorersWeb he is still considering his plans while observing the “crazy weather this season.” Moro attempted Manaslu in fall to acclimatize and become familiar with the terrain. However, like every other team, he had to call off the attempt due to dangerous conditions following extremely heavy snowfall. Moro wants to climb the peak in alpine style.

#8375. The Pressure to Crush Miles Can Ruin Your Thru-Hike. Don’t Let It.

After years of planning, you’re finally doing the thing: you’re thru-hiking! It’s exhilarating, it’s liberating, and it’s … remarkably stressful. You knew the trail would be hard, but now that you’re actually out there living the dream, you’re scared you won’t be able to keep up. The other thru-hikers seem stronger than you. More experienced. Younger. What if you fall behind and the whole thing falls apart?

This anxiety is familiar to many thru-hikers. We all know long-distance hiking is challenging, but we tend to picture spending six months walking through nature as a relaxing activity. So why do so many of us succumb to our fear of failure and spend the whole trip stressing about our mileage?

I’ve observed this behavior in countless thru-hikers, including myself at times. We’ll get to a beautiful viewpoint and stop to take a break, and after a few minutes, my hiking partner is already fidgeting and checking their watch. Or we’ll cross paths with a long-lost hiking friend and pause to chat before we go our separate ways, knowing we might not see each other again on that journey — yet my mind is only half on the conversation. The other half is running numbers and wondering how much this unplanned break will set me back.

Southern Maine on the AT was a lot harder than I expected and it slowed me down. But I just kept plugging away at the miles and finished anyway.

No one wants to still be stuck out on trail with miles to go before camp as darkness closes in — to say nothing of the fear of running out of food on the way to a planned resupply stop or not managing to complete the whole hike within that year’s weather window. As a result, there’s a tendency to rush.

I sometimes feel I can’t fully relax until I’ve gotten to my planned destination for the day. If I get there early, that just means I can push on a few more miles to make it even easier to reach the next day’s destination. And if I get there early, I can start building up a buffer of extra days in my schedule in case something goes wrong later on.

This instinct is arguably rooted in good sense. There are a lot of unknowns on a thru-hike and a lot of ways things can go wrong. But learning to live with the unknowns and adapt on the fly is also part of thru-hiking: in fact, I would argue that it’s one of the most crucial skills a thru-hiker must develop, full stop.

A lot can indeed go wrong in the course of a six-month thru-hike. But a lot can also go right in that same six months. If you suffer a setback on trail, chances are you will be able to make up for it over time. The most important thing is to not panic.

Getting “ahead” in your schedule might temporarily make you feel more in control, but this is largely an illusion. Pushing too hard could just as easily result in a hike-ending or hike-delaying overuse injury. Better to learn to live with the uncertainty and not let it ruin your day-to-day.

I’ve found that much of the joy and beauty of thru-hiking lies in the quiet moments of stillness: deep conversations shared with fellow hikers around camp, spontaneous fun on an unplanned zero day,  a particularly tasty snack enjoyed in solitude during a water break, a thousand spectacular sunrises and sunsets. If you’re so worried about the success or failure of your thru-hike that you have to sacrifice those moments just to feel like you’re still on track, what is even the point of being out there to begin with?

Remember: it’s OK to linger over a meal or enjoy a diverting side quest, even if it puts you behind your planned mileage for one day. Getting your miles in while the getting’s good is not a bad plan. But don’t let it sour the journey along the way.

#8370. The Paradox of Seeking First Ascents in Western Nepal

Western Nepal has plenty of unclimbed 6,000m peaks, and Fredrik Strang of Sweden and Sindre Kolbjornsgard of Norway went there planning to climb one. In the end, they settled for a slightly lower but equally memorable experience. It showed again that adventure goes beyond first ascents.

What I remember most clearly about that narrow summit is not the grade, the exposure, or the possibility of being first. It is the silence. No helicopters. No voices from a fixed-rope queue. No machinery, no aircraft, no distant sound of a settlement. Only the two of us, a serrated horizon, and an unfamiliar feeling that the mountain had asked a question rather than supplied an answer.

Sindre Kolbjornsgard, left, and Fredrik Strang. Photo: Fredrik Strang

After 18 expeditions to 8,000’ers and witnessing the evolution (or devolution) of climbing on these peaks’ normal routes, Strang and his partner knew they wanted something different. Quoting Ed Viesturs, Strang said: “The point is to climb, not just to summit.” With that in mind, the climbers set four criteria for their objectives:

Several route options face the climbers’ base camp tent. Photo: Fredrik Strang

Strang noted that there are many unclimbed peaks left in Nepal, but they were looking for a compelling climb, not just a dull summit for the record. They finally found one that satisfied their criteria, but then, as with so many other teams in Nepal this fall, harsh weather put their original objective out of reach. Not to mention that traveling Western Nepal is anything but simple.

“Our intended destination was in the Nyalu Lek area north of Simikot,” Strang revealed. “We planned to cross Nyalu La, a pass around 5,000m, with a support party that included porters and pack animals.

“Getting from Surkhet to Simikot took two rough days by road, with landslides having damaged or obliterated sections of the route. At Simikot, we learned that Nyalu La was probably impassable. Even reaching the place where we planned to start trekking had been uncertain.”

When they did reach the area, they confirmed that their planned peak was not an option. Hiking further down the valley, they pitched their tent at Phendol Kermi Camp. Snow had covered the trails beyond, but they simply had no time or money to move to some other region in Nepal. Instead, they decided to explore whatever was close to their camp.

During their stay, they encountered Mick Fowler and Victor Saunders of the UK. Bad weather had likewise spoiled the British pair’s plan to attempt an unclimbed 6,000m peak farther east, known only as Peak 6010, according to Mount Everest Foundation.. This would have been their second attempt on that peak. Ironically, dry conditions spoiled their 2025 attempt. This time, too much snow forced them back. Read more on the British climbers’ adventure here:

On October 6, Strang and Kolbjornsgard made their first acclimatization climb on a 5,177m peak at 30°20′49.82″N, 82°03′54.82″E. They found no records of any previous ascent.

“From base camp, the mountain looked straightforward, and lower down, it largely was,” Strang recalls. “Steep grass, mud, and broken rock led toward the upper slopes. But at about 4,500m, the route disappeared beneath knee-deep snow, then waist-deep snow, and every step became a small excavation.”

In the following days, they scouted and flew their drone down side valleys, looking for possibilities. Their second peak was 5,227m in altitude, located at 30°07′50.86″N, 81°41′56.58″E. Again, there were no records of previous ascents. Parts of it were far from fun.

“Below 4,500m, progress was tolerable, but above that, we were back to forcing our way through knee-deep, sometimes chest-deep snow,” Strang wrote. “A tremendous amount of work for very little enjoyment.”

Luckily, the climb improved once they reached the summit ridge, on relatively easy mixed rock and ice, which they assessed at PD+.

“Fowler and Saunders climbed the mountain several days later and found an easier way to descend and reascend the step on its western side,” Strang noted. “Their solution was a reminder that the first line a team takes is not necessarily the best one.”

Still, the peak that most drew the climbers’ attention was a remarkable 5,337m tooth of rock above Yangchya Lake at approximately 30°07′09.36″N, 81°41′21.15″E.

“We began calling it Daara Peak — a name inspired by the Nepali word for a projecting tooth or fang and by the mountain’s striking shape,” Strang said. He notes that the name is provisional while they await a response from the authorities about their suggestion.

Strang describes the peak as “a saber-toothed tiger’s canine protruding from a mass of rock. The terminal pinnacle was about eight meters high, overhanging and sharply defined against the sky.”

The climbers about to reach what they called Daara Peak. Drone photo: Brizendra Bhattarai

The problem was approaching the peak in deep, heavy snow from Yangchya Lake. They failed on their first attempt to tackle its northeast headwall. After waiting out another snowy spell, the climbers returned for a second attempt on October 17-18.

The climbers dealt with 250m of rather poor rock, a complex approach to the headwall across a bergschrund with soft snow, and the uncertainty of moving on unfamiliar terrain. They had no idea of the difficulties ahead or whether they could protect the passages ahead on their way to the summit. The route included vertical granite walls, with cracks adequate for cams, some mixed terrain with the crux at M6, a steep couloir, and then the summit ridge: a granite edge with some 30cm of snow on top.

Climbing terrain on Daara Peak. Photo: Fredrik Strang

Rather than technical difficulty, the section was delicate due to exposure and a lack of comfortable belay stations. Yet, the climbers reached the summit on October 18, including the top of the final pinnacle, thanks to a crack in the rock.

Strang admits that the climbing details suggest a rather straightforward ascent: a 5,337m summit via its northeast side in five pitches with difficulties up to M6. However, Strang judges the climb on a different scale. “The technical crux was behind us, but it was the part I remember most vividly,” he explained. “It was the silence.”

Strang and Kolbjornsgard’s route up Daara Peak. Photo: Fredrik Strang

On many of the 8,000m peaks I have climbed, the human presence has become part of the landscape: camps, radio calls, fixed ropes, queues, and the distant sound of aircraft. Up here, none of that reached us. Mountains extended in every direction. There was no audience, no ceremony, no one to confirm that we had accomplished anything at all.

Strang also reflects on the paradox: They enjoyed the wild terrain but, if every climber chases solitude by visiting these last remote valleys, the character of these places will inevitably change. For Strang, the question is not to ban access. However, he says:

Perhaps some summits should remain untouched — not because we lack the skill or courage to reach them, but because future generations deserve to inherit mountains that have not all been reduced to objectives.

The climb from the ridge. Photo: Fredrik Strang

#8366. A Climbing Expedition to 'Central Asia's Patagonia'

A mix of nine young and veteran Croatian climbers spent the month of August in one of the world’s great big-wall destinations — Kyrgyzstan’s Karavshin Range in the Pamir-Alay Mountains. Reaching up to 5,509m, the once-unknown granite cliffs now draw dozens of international climbers each summer. The two core valleys, Ak-Su and Kara-Su, have become known as Central Asia’s Patagonia.

The two leaders, Sinisa Skalec and Lukas Grbac Lackovic, spoke to ExplorersWeb about the place and their expedition. First, a summary of their four weeks.

Though suffering from stomach issues for most of the month (more on this later), the team repeated several granite classics, did a new route on 4,430m Pik Breeze, and attempted another new line.

Three climbers — Bruno Crljenic, Eva Pejic, and Lackovic — identified a potential new line below Pik Breeze’s west ridge. They knew of only one previous route on the mountain, done by Russians Marina Popova and Denis Prokofiev.

Beginning at 5am, the three crossed a broad scree slope, then began climbing a couloir below Pik Breeze’s west ridge. They negotiated loose rock, briefly followed an existing line, then moved left into crack systems.

Canned Horse, 6c A0, top. Below, previous attempts and possible other lines on the face.

They climbed until 9pm, when they bivouacked on a tiny ledge with space for only two people sitting and one lying down. Resuming at 8:30am, they reached a col after three pitches and continued directly up slabs and cracks. They finished on easier IV/V terrain and followed a 200m ridge to the summit.

They called their new line Canned Horse, 930m, 23 pitches, 6c A0. It took them a further eight hours to get back to base camp. During the climb, they found pitons on two pitches. They believe these belonged to another route on the west ridge, but the history of that line, and whether it was finished, is uncertain.

Pejic, Grbac Lackovic, and Crljenic on top of Pik Breeze.

Later in the month, one of those climbers, Eva Pejic, became quite ill and couldn’t leave base camp on her own. Five teammates helped evacuate her, carrying her for 11km, with assistance from other climbers in the area. She later recuperated in the Kyrgyz city of Osh.

On the first crux of ‘Perestroika Crack.’

Three small teams of Croatian climbers also repeated Perestroika Crack, one of the best-known long granite routes in Central Asia. It rises about 900m up the north face of 4,240m Pik Slesova and is graded 7a. Three members reportedly free-climbed the route. One pair, Sinisa Skalec and Ivan Vitez, completed the line in a single marathon day, beginning at 5:45am, summiting at 5:40pm, and returning to base camp at 11pm.

Skalec and Vitez also repeated the French Ridge of 4,510m Kyrkchilta, 2,000m, 6b to 6b+. They needed one bivouac. Toward the end of August, this same pair attempted a first ascent on the Central Pyramid of Ortotyubek, overlooking base camp. Their attempted route mounted slabs and cracks to the left of the established Take It Easy line, which other Croatians had repeated during that month. The pair gave up their attempt on August 26 because of illness.

Base camp with Ortotyubek and Slesova in the background.

Here is our interview with Lukas Grbac Lackovic and Sinisa Skalec about Kyrgyzstan and the Ak-Su Valley.

Lukas Grbac Lackovic repeats the Central Route on a peak called Small Russian Tower.

Was Eva Pejic’s health problem related to altitude or something else? What was the illness you experienced on Ortotyubek?

Eva’s health problem was unrelated to altitude exposure or the expedition environment. However, most of us experienced gastrointestinal infections, with symptoms including diarrhea, bloating, fever, and general malaise.

This significantly hindered our climbing, as everyone in the team got sick at least once, and some even twice. Recovery was slow and never quite complete –- we felt weak for most of the trip.

One thing that helped us recover was having plain rice with some of our meals, which we could get from the cook if we asked nicely. If we were to go again, we would definitely bring our own food and cooking equipment. This can be inconvenient, but it could potentially save you at least a week of being sick and unable to climb.

Another view of base camp and peaks Ortotyubek and Slesova.

Can you describe the Karavshin Valley? How large is it? Are there many side valleys?

The two main valleys are Ak-Su and Kara-Su. Adjacent to them is the Jaupaya Valley, which provides a descent route from Pik Breeze and is home to several peaks around 5,000m high. The rock quality there appears poor, and we are not aware of any established rock routes in the valley.

Another interesting area, west of Kara Su, is the Orto-Chashma Gorge. An Italian team made a first ascent there during our visit.

Here in the West, we first heard about the area following the kidnapping of four American climbers in Kara-Su in 2000. Since then, it seems to have calmed down and become a popular climbing destination. Is the area considered safe nowadays, or are there still things climbers should be aware of?

Currently, the security situation in the valley is good. There is always the possibility of tensions, of course, as the valleys lie close to the border with Tajikistan. However, in recent years, the number of climbers visiting the area has increased exponentially, reaching around 100 climbers this year.

How many other climbing teams were in Ak-Su and neighboring Kara-Su while you were there? Where were they generally from?

During the three weeks we spent in the valley, up to 50 climbers were in BC at the same time. Climbers came from all over the world — Chile, U.S., Spain, Slovakia, Poland, Belgium, Slovenia, France, Italy, Germany, Japan, Russia…

We had originally planned a different expedition, but had to change our destination just a few months before departure. Some friends from Croatia and Slovenia recommended the area because of its straightforward logistics and relatively good security, while still offering impressive big walls and proper crack climbing. It didn’t take much to convince us!

Are there any military checkpoints? Do you need special permission to enter the valleys?

Yes, you have to pass through a military checkpoint when entering the area. However, the outfitter handles the application for the necessary permits and ensures everything goes smoothly.

Some call the Karavshin Valley the Patagonia of Central Asia because of its aesthetic granite walls. Do you think that’s a fair description?

Patagonia is definitely more spectacular, but you pay the price with poor weather. If your goal is to climb almost every day, then the Karavshin Valley is a better choice.

Climbing in Patagonia requires much more logistical planning and preparation, and the approaches themselves are a whole different story. In the Karavshin Valley, on the other hand, there is no snow or ice during the season we visited (August), at least on the walls we climbed. Some of the walls are just a 15-minute walk from BC, and you can reach them all in approach shoes.

Perestroika Crack and some of the classic routes in the Karavshin region are arguably just as good as the best rock routes in Patagonia.

How does the granite compare to Yosemite and Patagonia?

The granite is more similar in texture to that found in Patagonia; it is not as smooth as in Yosemite. The overall rock quality is generally good, although, as everywhere, some sections are of poorer quality. One downside of the mild climate in the Karavshin Valley is the dirt and grass that accumulate in the cracks, which can sometimes detract from the aesthetic appeal of the routes. The more popular and frequently climbed routes have already been cleaned and are pleasant to climb.

You climbed 4-1/2 pitches of the route on Ortotyubek. How much did you have left to complete it?

There were still two-and-a-half pitches left to complete the route up to the junction with Take It Easy. We envisioned the second half of the fifth pitch following the line up to a point just below the overhang that runs diagonally to the left.

From there, the sixth pitch follows a thin crack, from which you need to traverse left and move into another system of thin cracks that runs across the roof and joins the Take It Easy belay (seventh pitch). The last pitch of Take It Easy offers a logical exit, and we don’t think there is any need to come up with an alternative.

At the point where we stopped (first half of the fifth pitch), we left two pitons that we used as a temporary rappel anchor. Repeating parties are welcome to remove them, as they were only left for temporary use. We think a few bolts may be needed in the second half of the fifth pitch, but that obviously depends on the abilities of those planning to complete the route.

All belays are equipped (the first and fourth belays have two 8mm bolts each, while the second and third have two pitons each). In addition, we left two or three pitons in the first pitch and two in the second pitch.

As in the rest of the valley, some sections of the route are filled with dirt and grass. We made an effort to clean the cracks in the first four pitches, but there is still plenty of work to be done, especially on the sixth pitch, which we didn’t climb, where a thin crack is completely filled with dirt.

How much unclimbed rock remains? Are the obvious lines already established, or are there still many promising routes?

The most obvious and accessible lines may have already been climbed, but there is still plenty of potential. Anyone willing to put in the effort can establish a new route. The area is vast, and there is still plenty of room for new routes.

Your website mentions that there are guidebooks to certain routes in that area. Where are these available?

Most of the guidebooks we used are available online. We received some Russian guidebooks from climbing friends, although we didn’t use them very much. We’re not sure how easily they can be found online. Climbers from all over the world bring various materials to the camp, so most route topos and information can be obtained there.

What was the most unexpected experience on your expedition — something that might surprise climbers familiar with other big-wall areas?

We were pleasantly surprised by the kindness and honesty of the Kyrgyz people. When traveling to remote parts of the world, many of us tend to expect that someone will try to rip us off and that we will have to haggle over everything, but that was not the case here.

Although some things took longer than expected, everything we had agreed on in advance was respected, and all the logistics for transportation and accommodation worked very well.

As we mentioned earlier, our only complaint concerns the food and hygiene conditions at the camp, which were most likely responsible for the digestive problems experienced by virtually all the climbers staying there.

#8362. Avalanche Fatality Warns About Early Ski Conditions In The Alps

Little snow on the mountains doesn’t mean safe conditions. An American off-piste skier died in the Austrian Alps last weekend after he triggered a small slab avalanche. It was far too small to bury him, but it carried him into an open crevasse below.

With the ski season barely underway, this is Europe’s first avalanche victim this season. Last year, 151 people died in avalanches in Europe between October 2025 and June 2026, according to the European Avalanche Warning Service (EAWS), a shockingly high number.

Most victims perished in the Alps: 40 in Italy, 35 in France, 33 in Austria, and 18 in Switzerland. It was the 13th most deadly year in the Alps since record-keeping began. It was also the highest tally ever since the “Winter of Terror” of 1951. Avalanche prevention standards have improved a lot since then, but the number of leisure skiers, climbers, and hikers in the mountains has multiplied as well. (Most of those 1951 victims lived in villages along avalanche paths.)

Last weekend’s accident took place at the Stubai Glacier ski resort. The glacier sections of the Alps typically open for skiing weeks earlier than other mountain resorts, thanks to their higher altitudes and glacial ice, which can provide good October skiing with just a thin layer of fresh snow on top. Stubai’s ski resort opened on October 9 this year.

A map of Stubai Glacier ski resort with the area where the accident happened circled in red. Photo: Stubaier Gletscher website

The skier was on his own, descending in an out-of-bounds area below East Daunkogel Peak at around 11:30am. His tracks on the snow show he eventually abandoned the snow-covered glacier and ventured onto a steeper, rocky area. At some point, he broke a small slab of crusty snow which dragged him some 50 meters into an open bergschrund, where he fatally fell 20 meters down, according to the Lawinen Report.

The accident site, with the skier’s tracks visible,  and the movement of the snow slab — 50m long and 25m wide — marked in pink. Photo: Lawinen Report

Other skiers in the area saw the accident and raised the alarm, but the skier had died by the time they extracted him from the crevasse. The police said the slab was only 10cm to 30cm thick, and the slide was just 25 meters wide. The crevasse was 50 meters below the fracture point.

Avalanche risks are obvious on heavily loaded slopes, but the accident shows that even a thin layer of unstable snow can cause a fatal fall. In this case, the snow had fallen recently on the verglass ice over glacier-polished smooth rocks, and had no time to settle. This is a typical early-season condition in mountain ranges around the world.

The accident occurred at nearly 3,000m of altitude on a shady northeast slope, where the snow hardly transforms and settles during the short days of late fall. To make things worse, the report notes that wind had picked up that morning, creating a weak crust on top of loose, cold, fresh snow, prone to breaking.

The avalanche site on the following day, with most of the terrain covered by freshly drifted snow. Photo: LWD Tirol

The second factor was exposure: the skier might have easily survived the fall if the terrain had been a clean snow slope, but he was on rocky terrain, where a simple fall can result in serious injuries. Most of all, the crevasse below created what the report described as a “terrain trap.”

Fans of backcountry and ski touring are eager to hit the slopes with the first snowflakes, and the scarcely covered terrain may provide a false sense of safety from avalanches. But objective dangers go beyond the big powder avalanches and also include falls on icy slopes. In addition, the glaciers are dry after the summer, and the crevasses are wide open.

After a mild fall, snow is falling heavily in the Alps this week, significantly improving conditions for the region’s ski resorts. Most of them plan to open this weekend. The snow will also offer backcountry opportunities, but conditions will remain highly unstable.

Snowfall up to two meters is expected today in the Alps. Graphic by meteoexploration.com

The avalanche report today by the Tiroler Avalanche Service (LWD Tirol) shows low risk in the Austrian mountains, a remarkable risk (3 out of 5) in the Swiss Alps, and moderate risk (2 out of 5) in France.

The avalanche forecast for today, November 19, in the Alps shows remarkable (level 3-orange) risk, especially in Switzerland. Graphic: LWD Tirol

#8358. Family Offers $75,000 Reward to Save Climber Missing on Mount Fuji

Today, November 19, the Yamanashi Prefectural Police announced that they had ended the search for Chinese climber Chen Jie, 25, according to the Japanese national newspaper Mainichi Shimbun. Chen disappeared November 8 on the main Yoshida Trail after continuing alone up 3,776m Mount Fuji during its closed season.

His two companions reportedly turned back because of deteriorating weather and inadequate equipment. Chen continued on his own without crampons or sufficient cold-weather clothing. His last video was sent that morning between 2,300 and 2,700m.

His father subsequently traveled to Japan and offered a reward of RMB500,000 ($75,000) for information leading to his recovery alive, or RMB100,000 ($15,000) for recovery of his body.

Ironically, Chen belonged to China’s Blue Sky Rescue Team, a volunteer search-and-rescue organization. His mother told local media that he had participated in rescues in China and had some mountaineering experience, including trekking and climbing in Nepal and Indonesia.

#8353. Climbers Forge New Route on Mount Shiva Despite Limited Acclimatization

Benjamin Bosshard and Philippo Sala will never forget their first experience above 6,000m and the new route they opened with Stefan Siegrist on India’s Bahai Jar, commonly known as Mount Shiva (6,142m).

Expeditions in the Indian Himalaya are usually quiet while they take place, because satellite phones and InReach devices are prohibited. After returning home, however, Stefan Siegrist reported the details, and the team’s cameraman, Christoph Detschmann, posted a video summary of the expedition:

Siegrist had already visited the Chenab River Valley area in 2018 and climbed Shiva with Jonas Schild, but he still had designs on its unclimbed northwest ridge. At the end of September, he, Sala, and Bosshard reached base camp in the Kishtwar massif.

The three Swiss climbers were prepared to endure a long period of bad weather while acclimatizing. To their surprise, a good weather window opened right away. It was too good to let go, despite not being properly acclimatized and Sala and Bosshard’s lack of altitude experience. The window was expected to last just three days. After many “discussions and doubts,” they left base camp on October 3.

Sala had a headache during the first night, but the following morning, they were all totally focused on the climb, and the tension disappeared. “We assumed that we were unlikely to reach the summit on this attempt, and that we would therefore be wasting our only chance before a major storm [brought] the season to an end,” Siegrist explained. “So from then on, the idea was simply to climb higher and acclimatize, without any pressure.”

A moment of the climb, filmed from a drone by Christoph Detschmann

Along the way, they discovered they had left their stove at base camp. No problem in 2026: The expedition photographer used his drone to carry the stove up to them. The use of drones was a hot topic during the recent Piolets d’Or: To what extent are they compatible with alpine-style criteria? While most accepted that drones could scout routes or sections out of view of base camp, many considered using them to carry equipment up a face to be a red line.

On Shiva, Siegrist says the delivery of the missing stove “proved essential to the success of the climb.”

The climbers spent their second night at 5,250m at the base of the northwest ridge. On the following morning, they had to decide whether to continue or retreat. They all felt well, but starting the highly technical ridge was a point of no return. At the same time, Siegrist recalls, they realized they really had a chance to summit. And so on they went.

That night, they stopped at 5,700m in what Siegrist describes as a crucial moment. His partners had not been at that altitude before, and the latest forecast announced a storm the following day. They decided to wait and see what the morning looked like. No one slept at all that night.

The last meters before the summit. Drone image by Christoph Detschmann

The sky was still clear when the team set off again at 4am, so they chose to keep going. “After a while, we finally reached the final slope, just 300m below the summit,” Siegrist wrote. By now, they knew they were going to make it. They reached the top at 7:44am, six days after arriving in Base Camp, and just in time to hurry down as the storm approached.

The climbers descended via the 1985 Japanese route (see topo below), and reached their base camp tents as it started to snow.

#8352. What’s in My Pack…

Well, let’s see. There’s raingear, gloves, hat, a blanket, sweatshirt, a calculus book, some water…

Yes. I also have my astronomy and chemistry books in there. Back when I was in college – before the internet but after color TV was apparently invented – our college professors assured us we would all be using calculus in our engineering careers. I’ve wondered for decades when I would ever use this… material (putting it politely), other than to teach it to my son or other engineering students who struggled with higher-level math. So, after thirty-five years, I’ve finally found a use for it.

I don’t expect to be calculating any derivatives out on the trail, though I suppose there could be some deep analysis on rates of change over time, especially involving hiking distances per day.

For astronomy, I love looking at the stars. Sure, it’s engineering astronomy with lots of galactic calculations for weights, trajectories and distances, but it has a few very pretty star charts that would look great at night. Not so much at 10 a.m. on a random Saturday, but considering Michigan, the probability of unusual weather events is never zero.

What about chemistry? Its really more of a canary in a coal mine for me… or more accurately, a canary in my backpack. The only chemical reaction I’m investigating is whether the chemistry book turns out wet and its pages become more pulp-like, in which case I’ve learned something.

I’d take my statistics book, which is a heavier, but I actually like that one. Yes, I know. I have a bit of a twisted mind to enjoy statistics. The other choice was my Engineering Project Management book. While hiking the AT is, in itself, an entire project management adventure, and I suspect Change Control may be a solid fireside topic while hiking, I still need that book for work-related activities.

A better question may be WHY do I have these three books in my pack?

Weight. They help my pack get up to 30 pounds, which I hope is my peak hiking weight when I’m on the trail next March. The calculus book is a whomping 5 pound and a touch over 15 ounces.  Lots of “good times” in that book.  Chemistry is another five pounds and almost 2 ounces while astronomy is in between with 5 pounds and 5 ounces.

Perhaps a better title for this post would be “How Am I Preparing for My AT Hike?” In which case, those books are involved, but no, they aren’t going on the trail with me in four months.

For preparing my body for the trail, there are three strategies I’m using:

Southeastern Michigan doesn’t have mountains, and the hills are more bump-like, but they are there. Tossing a 30-pound pack on my back and hiking 5–6 miles is a decent warm-up. I’m trying to do that every week.

Right now, I just finished a five-day continuous stretch of doing this every morning, as I had some vacation time still to burn from work. I’m assessing how my body handles it, what that strange feeling is in my legs, why my ankles are sore, and trying to force myself to get up, out of a comfortable bed, and hike in sub-30-degree weather. It’s been challenging but so far, OK. I am glad, though, to take a break over the next few days and instead keep working on the other two strategies.

Besides just working on my body, I’m also testing how various software works while on day hikes – my Garmin In-Reach Mini has passed my previous checks and now has its subscription suspended for another few months until I really need it, but testing Day One (a journaling app), Grammarly (to well… help with my grammar) and hopefully, WordPress to see how a post or two work here when I’m coming off a hike when I tired, hungry and just want to start my drive home with the heat on full blast.

What would be considered the easiest is actually one of the harder ones for me. A good workout at the gym is two hours. That’s enough time to get at least three miles on the treadmill (at 3.4 mph with a 6–7° uphill grade), core work, strength training, stretching and maybe finishing by laying on a hydro lounger at the end.

Sadly, my job takes up longer hours than I want to admit at times, but at least I enjoy doing what I am doing at the office as well as the people I work with. The problem comes at the end of the day. If I don’t leave early enough, I don’t get to the gym until after 5 p.m., in which case it’s impossible to get a decent work out and get home in time to cook dinner for my wife. I’m left wondering where the day went.

Yes, it’s true I could get up earlier in the morning, but… that isn’t happening. Probably won’t happen on the trail either, to be fair. Getting up before the sun rises is something I consider a necessary evil to continue getting a paycheck. Getting up even earlier to willingly work out is far worse and would fall into the category of a malicious act of cruelty to my body.

This is strangely enough, the easiest and most satisfying. I’m doing a routine of about thirty minutes with ankle strengthening, core work and stretching. It’s something casual to do while watching TV and the time just passes. It’s not the most useful, but hopefully it will help prevent something like an ankle sprain.

As for my actual gear list. Yes, I’ll post it. It will probably be right after the Christmas holidays, as I have some new gear that absolutely needs to be weighed, manhandled and experimented with. My hope is less than 20 pounds base weight for starting in March, with a fully loaded pack of under 30 pounds. Whether I hit that target or not, is in jeopardy with the requirement of a bear can, but that’s another discussion…

About me? Sure. I’m a native Detroiter and have lived my whole life in Michigan where I live with my wife – more than 25 years – and a couple of college-aged children. Well, technically the kids live off at college but they do come home to make the house look a natural disaster struck while we weren’t looking. I’m an engineer, working for one of the Big Three automakers and have well over 30 years of experience doing everything from breaking transmissions to quality improvements and even designing cooling systems for both trucks and cars. Outside of work, I love exploring and spending time outdoors. I’ve learned a lot about camping over the last few decades, including relearning wonderful lessons like not leaving an unlocked cooler in camp and proper flow directions on my water filter. Somewhere in there, I fell in love with backpacking and found a whole new world of mistakes I can learn from. Eventually, I discovered long-distance thru-hiking and convinced both my job and my family that taking a vacation from me for six months would be beneficial to them (suckers!). Catch me on a good day, and I’d be happy to talk about camping, backpacking, video games, books, music or just about anything else fun. Just don’t ask me about spreadsheets, checklists, FMEAs or change control meetings.

I thought the books were reading material while you wait for rescue after breaking your ankle after falling down a ravine… ;-P No – wait, if I were stuck reading calculus I’d just want to end it right then and there…

#8347. Two Inexperienced Teens Rescued After 20 Hours on Grossglockner

Two Germans, aged 15 and 18, spent almost 20 hours on Austria’s highest mountain before being evacuated by helicopter on November 15.

Initially, police reported that the pair had reached the 3,798m summit and become lost while descending. The younger climber disputes this, saying they turned back near an alpine hut at 3,454m because his companion felt ill.

Their ordeal began around 11pm on Saturday, November 14. The pair had no previous experience with such a serious mountain but had prepared by reading websites, watching videos, training physically, and asking others for tips. They did carry crampons, an ice axe, a helmet, a rope, a belay device, and extra clothing.

It took them a long time before they decided to turn around. The descent went well at first, but one spot seemed too dangerous to them. To get around it, they followed someone else’s tracks in the snow, but these suddenly disappeared. While looking for a way, they got stuck in deep snow. The older boy called for help at around 6:30pm on November 15, according to Austria’s public broadcaster, ORF.at.

At first, rescuers tried to guide the pair down by phone. More than two hours later, the boys were still stuck, so a helicopter was dispatched. The rescuers found the pair, exhausted, disoriented, and hypothermic, at around 2,800m.

A rescue helicopter brings the teens to safety. Photo: Mountain Rescue KALS

Yesterday, rescue leader Peter Tembler criticized their lack of alpine experience and preparation. He told the German Press Agency that the pair lacked sufficient experience for the terrain and winter conditions. He also criticized their late-night departure.

According to Tembler, a section that normally takes four to five hours took them almost 12. Other climbers reportedly advised them against continuing.

Tembler believes an increasing number of inexperienced people are attempting serious alpine routes, sometimes encouraged by social media accounts that downplay the difficulty. The disagreement has become a public debate about risk-taking, responsibility, and rescue operations.

As Austria’s highest peak, Grossglockner is a magnet for climbers of all stripes and has more than its share of controversy. In January 2025, a man abandoned his less experienced girlfriend high on the mountain. She froze to death, and an Austrian court later convicted him of manslaughter for leaving her behind. This summer, an altercation occurred on Grossglockner in which a guide insulted a passing climber and nearly pushed him off a cliff. At the same time, veteran alpinists are still setting bold new routes here.

According to Der Standard, Grossglockner gets 8,000 to 9,000 ascents each year, with an average of two dozen rescues annually. Between 2005 and 2025, 29 climbers have died on the mountain.

#8344. Weekend Warm-Up: Hurricane Chase

This episode of the storm-chasing TV series Storm Rising is titled “High Plains Insanity.” Produced by National Geographic, it follows Reed Timmer and Mike Theiss as they attempt to navigate and document an increasingly unpredictable storm season.

The storm-chasing segments are filmed like an action movie but, as Timmer makes clear, thrills are not the primary objective. As the climate changes and disrupts weather patterns, tornadoes are no longer limited to traditional seasons and ranges.

“That’s why we need to be on the ground directly in the path of these tornadoes,” Timmer explains, “to record data that no one else is getting.”

Driving into a potential tornado in Montana. Photo: Screenshot

With hurricane and tornado seasons now overlapping, the duo is forced to split up to cover the widest possible area and collect the most data. For the tornadoes, this means deploying a probe into the funnel.

Up north in the High Plains of the U.S. West and Midwest, Timmer and his dog Gizmo narrowly miss storm after storm. Gizmo is better company but is a very poor navigator, while Timmer isn’t much better. He constantly makes wrong turns as he tries to navigate, drive, and prepare equipment. He does take the time to explain the basic weather science behind what he is failing to catch, such as the conditions that created the baseball-sized hail pummeling his windshield.

Timmer and Gizmo drive through the aftermath of a powerful tornado in the Black Hills of North Dakota. Photo: Screenshot

In Florida, Theiss sleeps in his car to maintain a constant vigil along the coast. Our current scientific abilities, he explains, allow us to track the movement of hurricane systems with decent accuracy. But predicting their strength is much more difficult. Systems can suddenly turn deadly or fizzle out with equally short notice. In this case, the terrible-looking storm comes to nothing. He heads back up north to rejoin Timmer and Gizmo.

Gizmo buffeted by fierce winds. Photo: Screenshot

The reunited trio prepares for a final effort, complete with a windshield-replacement sequence. They immediately drive into the gathering storm, passing through a hail core which, of course, destroys the new windshield. The Lord giveth and taketh away, et cetera. Soon they’re racing on a near-empty tank, as the powerful storm threatens to touch down at any moment.

It’s their last chance this season to deploy the probe. When, after a long, tense chase, they actually manage to do it, both erupt into cheers. Gizmo appears unmoved, despite the fact that this ground probe, deployed in a storm of this type, in this area, has never been deployed before and is sure to yield valuable scientific data.

Lou Bodenhemier holds an MA in History from the University of Limerick and a BA in Creative Writing from the University of Arizona. He’s interested in maritime and disaster history as well as criminal history, and his dissertation focused on the werewolf trials of early modern Europe. At the present moment he can most likely be found perusing records of shipboard crime and punishment during the Age of Sail, or failing that, writing historical fiction horror stories. #8343. Escaping the Farting Ghost Hotel: 17.6 Miles into Portugal

We both thought the place we slept in last night was haunted. It was on the backside of a thousand-year-old church, with one wall actually serving as the back of the altar. We both woke up in the middle of the night feeling really hot and smelling a sewer odor. Knockerz had some strange dreams, as did I.

When we left, my phone died as I tried to disconnect from the Wi-Fi. After a restart, Knockerz’s phone suddenly started talking to her—something it never does.

We headed out around 7:00 AM while it was still in the high 50s. We also lost an hour crossing the water: Spain keeps the same time all the way out, but when you drop into Portugal, the clocks go back an hour. A high-speed train barreled by shortly after we set off.

We’ve been navigating our own Camino route choices since entering Portugal, generally following the official routes. This has allowed us to get off the beaten path, explore the backcountry, and see areas untouched by millions of pilgrims over the centuries. Of course, self-made routes sometimes come with obstacles, like busy highways with no shoulder.

At one point, I pulled up a map and realized we were on the coastal route. We’ve been bouncing between the coastal route (slightly inland and more popular) and the littoral route (which hugs the coastline and isn’t on many maps) because they run so close together.

We stopped at a cafe for some caffeine and breakfast treats. The pastries here are different from Spanish treats—more layered, like a croissant, and only slightly sweet. I also noticed people saying “bom caminho” instead of the Spanish “buen camino.”

The people here are very friendly, constantly greeting us with bom dia (good day). We’ve started practicing our basic Portuguese greetings:

We bumped back out to the coast where the littoral and coastal paths briefly share a path. A cool coastal fog sheltered us from the sun as the air warmed into the 60s.

We enjoyed the littoral route past a wide beach featuring an old fort—its design looked remarkably similar to a fort we visited in St. Augustine, Florida. After that, we walked on a long boardwalk through a marshy area for several miles.

Near Âncora, we took a littoral path out to the coast that forced us to walk through heavy sand dunes. It was exhausting, so we decided to bail and take an alternate route along a busy road.

After walking about a mile of cars whizzing past on a narrow sidewalk (and climbing about 500 feet off the beach), I found a quieter parallel road winding through local villages.

At this point, we were starving, so we found a restaurant that served a wonderful, incredibly cheap meal. Afterward, we made our way back to the coast to rejoin the littoral route.

We walked through farm fields on a narrow path paved with six-inch rocks, much like an old Roman road we traveled in Spain. Our path shifted through a mix of paved tracks, cobblestones, and large boulders. With the fog mostly burned off, the sun rays grew hot, but a constant, cold ocean breeze kept us comfortable. Most of the coastline here is rocky, dotted with tidal pools.

As we approached our final destination, we could spot a castle up on the hill and what looked like a grand structure on the same hilltop. It had been a long, 17-mile day, and we were both completely exhausted.

We finally arrived in Viana do Castelo, a very cool medieval town that happened to be hosting a massive medieval (and Renaissance) festival! We wandered around for a while, taking in all the people dressed and acting like historical figures.

Tired out, we found a place to sit, enjoy some Portuguese-sized glasses of red wine, and people-watch for a couple of hours. It was actually quite cold, even in the middle of June!

We finally headed to our room, which happened to be located in the basement. Honestly, it was perfect—we were so tired and ready for some rest. Especially Knockerz, who needed to sleep off the memory of the farting ghost hotel from the night before!

Richard Carlos Skidmore, 66, of the United States, was found dead in his tent on Mera Peak on Sunday, November 22, after summiting the 6,476m mountain the previous morning.

According to Solukhumbu district police, he reached the summit at approximately 10am on Saturday, November 21, and descended to the high camp at around 5,800m, where he spent the night.

#8335. Preparing for 2200….Because One Does Not Simply “Pop Out for a bit of a Hike”

Preparing for a thru hike on Appalachian Trail truly begins with just one burning question;  “What will I actually need to walk 2200 miles?”   That’s pretty simple and straightforward right?  Theoretically, yes………that is, of course, until you discover the mind-numbing multitude of content creator gear videos.

Suddenly, you find yourself manically comparing sleeping bags by their temperature rating, researching water filters like you’re prepping for the apocalypse, and obsessing over the ratio of weight and R-rating of every single sleeping pad in existence. Your hike is still months away, but you’ve already downloaded four GPS trail apps, scheduled transportation,  meticulously planned your daily mileage to the foot and plotted every daily campsite  down to the hour of  arrival.

Relax……You’re definitely not the first, or the last hiker to become immersed (obsessed?) in the vortex that is thru hiking prep!  Perhaps I can break it down and make it a little more palatable

First comes the backpack. It should be light, durable, comfortable, and large enough to hold everything you need—which, according to differing opinions, is both nothing and several highly specialized pieces of equipment. First, try the pack on in the store. Bring your gear, (yes, really do this) load up the pack you’re interested in, and then look yourself wearing it the in the mirror. Pay attention at how it feels.  Walk around to see how securely it sits.  Then, ask yourself….do I look ready to summit a mountain or preparing to flee a small country?  Adjust your choice according to what you see and feel.   Lastly, never, ever choose your pack based on the popularity of it, the aesthetics, or because the unsolicited opinion of some random internet blogger.

Then there’s your shelter. You want something weatherproof, spacious, easy to set up, and light enough that you won’t begin to question your life choices by mile four. Picture this;  You finally pull the trigger on the tent;  the eager  salesperson assures you that it’s really simple to pitch. You proudly take it home and then spend twenty five minutes trying to decipher the pitching instructions, and ultimately end up with what, oddly, looks like a very expensive kite!  Key advice: Research. research, research!  Take your time, debate with your eager brain. and finally choose the “one” based solely on what YOUR hiking style looks like. With so many options and opinions out there, only your opinion matters!

The art of  deciding if a sleeping bag or quilt…..down or synthetic …….or temperature rating, is for you, is another deeply personal decision.  When and where are you starting?  Average temperatures where you’ll be at that time of year?   Lightweight or no?  Inflatable pad or closed foam?  Answer these questions, imagine scenarios,  and the decision will be much clearer.

Food actually takes up surprisingly little space…..that is,  until you remember you’ll need to eat it every day. Focus on a balance of carbs, protein, and pleasure.

As a novice, I bought some of those fancy dehydrated meals labeled “creamy pasta primavera,” or “Spaghetti with meat sauce”.  I added the correct amount of boiling water, and soon I discovered that the words “creamy” or “meat” were undoubtedly creative writing! Still, in all fairness , it did have calories, and, in the end, calories are the fuel of the trail.

Clothing……now this decision becomes just another expedition into the unknown. Basically, you need layers for warmth, rain protection, sun protection, and the full understanding that your clothes may never again smell like laundry.

I pack two shirts; one for hiking, and one for sleeping, two pair of socks, two underwear, and one pair of long pants and one pair of shorts.  That’s it, because apparently I’m going into the wilderness, not to a four-day business conference.

Finally, you weigh your pack. You realize that it weighs enough that to suddenly start to reconsider your plans, question all of your hiking friendships, and immediately begrudge the person who told you that hiking was “just walking.” You remove a book, a camp mug, and a backup pair of pants. Then you eventually load them back because what if you want coffee while reading in clean pants?  I mean….that makes sense right??

Pick the gear you bring and the total weight of the full kit solely on what you’re honestly willing to carry.

The key, you’ll learn, is to pack what you need, to test it BEFORE you leave, and accept that your first big purchase may be a tiny scale. The Appalachian Trail doesn’t care whether your gear matches. It cares if you can carry it safely, use it efficiently, and still keep walking when your feet have begun filing formal complaints !

So, you now shoulder your pack, you take a few determined steps around the block, feeling great about your newfound expertise, and feel like you’re ready for anything……..but then you remember your loaded food bag is still sitting on the kitchen table.  Ugh!

For reference, I have included pictures of my full gear setup in hopes it will give you some reference.   GOOD LUCK!

#8334. New Route on Classic Tien Shan Peak

Three Polish climbers have established a new line on the north face of one of the Tien Shan’s best-known climbing peaks.

Michal Makowski, Robert Paluch, and Rafal Zając took 11 hours to climb their new 850m line on 4,777m Free Korea Peak, in Kyrgyzstan’s northern Tien Shan Mountains. They then spent a further 11 hours returning to base camp.

They named the route The Polish Barber, after pioneer American climber Henry Barber, who soloed the wall in 1976. Their line shares the first 250–300m with Barber’s, Makowski told ExplorersWeb.

“According to the information I have, [the remaining 600-650m] was previously unclimbed and had never been attempted by another team,” said Makowski. “We reached the summit ridge and then began rappelling down from there.

Corona Hut, the team’s base camp. Photo: Polski Związek Alpinizmu

Free Korea Peak — Pik Svobodnaya Koreya in Russian — was already famous among mountaineers in the former Soviet Union because of its 900m north wall. in 2018, Russian climber Valery Balesin suggested that it was no longer possible to find new lines on this well-known face, although advances in steep ice-climbing techniques have clearly opened new possibilities.

“My friends and I researched Free Korea Peak and realized that part of the north face still has unclimbed terrain,” said Makowski.

On the Polish Barber route. Photo: Polski Związek Alpinizmu

Their route was almost completely ice climbing. The crux came midway up the wall, when they faced a particularly steep section of ice that they graded at Alpine Ice 4+. The rest of the route was 3/3+. Fortunately, “protection on the Polish Barber was really good, except for the last 150m, where ice was pretty thin and crusty,” said Makowski.

Climbing by moonlight. Photo: Polski Związek Alpinizmu

Despite its former popularity, they had the valley almost to themselves during their week in camp. There was just one Russian group doing a tourist trek up nearby Corona Peak.

A scrambly section on Free Korea Peak. Photo: Polski Związek Alpinizmu

#8330. Ukrainian Solos New Route in Gokyo Valley, Near Everest

Mykyta Balabanov of Ukraine has soloed a new route on the northeast face of Nepal’s Phari Lapcha (6,017m). Also known as Machhermo Peak, it sits 24km west of Everest in the Gokyo Valley.

Balabanov is still trekking back to Lukla, but has given ExplorersWeb some details and photos about this impressive new route.

The Ukrainian set off on his own up an unclimbed line on the northeast face on November 19. He made two bivouacs on the way up and one more on the descent.

“The level of difficulty is hard to tell, as always when solo, but I’d say it was around 80° on ice, M5+, 5c on rock, and lots of poor snow!” Balavanov said.

He estimates the new route is 1,200m long, and spans some 850 vertical meters from base to summit.

Rough topo of Balabanov’s solo route on the northeast face of Phari Lapcha. Photo: Mykyta Balabanov

Another side of Phari Lapcha saw action just one day before Balabanov, when U.S. guide Bennie Lieber led Canadian Emma Deguara up the Stone(d) Yeti route on the south face.

“I was not related to that climb, as I climbed alone after approaching from a different valley,” Balabanov explained. “However, I saw their tracks on the summit and spotted their bivy place at the bottom of the south face.”

Lieber and Deguara made the second ascent of their chosen route. “While the technical grade (M3, AI2+) is easily digestible, the room for mistakes, due to exposure, is zero,” Lieber said.

Mykyta Balabanov and fellow Ukrainian Mikhail Fomino opened a new route on Ama Dablam in 2024, but they first became widely known for their new route on the Southeast Ridge of Annapurna III in 2021.

#8328. Bears, Moldy Gear & Navigation Mishaps: My First Solo Backpacking Adventure on the Florida Trail

There’s something empowering about stepping into the wilderness alone, knowing that whatever happens, you’re the one who has to figure it out.

For my first-ever solo backpacking trip, I set out to hike a 60 mile section of the Florida Trail through the Ocala National Forest and Juniper Wilderness Area. I’ve spent thousands of miles backpacking alongside Lane, often leaning on his experience and confidence in the backcountry. This time, I wanted to put my own skills to the test. I wanted to see what it felt like to navigate the challenges, make the decisions, and handle whatever the trail threw at me without someone else to lean on.

What I didn’t anticipate was just how much the trail would throw at me in four short days. What started as a simple, well-planned backpacking trip, quickly turned into some of the most challenging days I’ve ever experienced on the trail and with so many things going wrong.

Between a mold-infested sleeping bag, curious black bears (including a face-to-face encounter), countless tick and chigger bites, sleepless cold nights, unexpected detours due to navigational mistakes, and a few genuinely beautiful stretches of wilderness, this trip turned into an adventure I won’t soon forget.

More importantly, it built a confidence in myself that I hadn’t fully tapped into before. I discovered that I really enjoy the solitude, the independence, and the sense of empowerment that comes with figuring things out on my own.

My dad dropped me off at Rodman Dam around 1:30 p.m., after we first cached some water at the County Road 316 crossing. I headed north through the tall longleaf pine forests, with sections of lightly overgrown trail scattered throughout the afternoon.

I encountered only two northbound hikers during the first few miles, and they would turn out to be the only hikers I’d see over the entire 60-mile stretch. Within the first hour, I also came across some fresh bear scat, a friendly little reminder that I was no longer walking through the Florida I was accustomed to growing up here in the Sunshine State.

I made it about seven miles before finding a spot off-trail to set up camp around 5:30 p.m. I could hear ATVs riding throughout the area, and rather than push on toward the campground, I decided to call it a day and settle in so I could enjoy some reading in the tent before dinner.

That’s when things started getting interesting.

After setting up camp, I discovered that my sleeping bag had developed mold all over it since the last time I’d used it. Awesome.

So, I laid the bag outside on the ground beside my tent to start drying before I would pack it away in my backpack and hope it wouldn’t get cold enough that I would actually need it.

After prepping dinner in my tent, which consisted of cold soaking some ramen in a talenti ice cream container, I heard sniffing around my tent. I turned around and found myself practically eye-to-eye with a black bear investigating my moldy sleeping bag.

My first reaction was to yell, “Get out of here bear!” Making my voice deeper and louder with each attempt at repeating this chant. It jumped back, startled by my yelling.

I grabbed my bear spray, got out of the tent, and yelled until it eventually wandered off. It kept stopping to look back at me curiously before disappearing out of sight. Not exactly the wildlife encounter I’d been hoping for on my first solo night.

I packed up my food and ate dinner a good distance away from camp, making sure to keep everything bear-proofed.

Naturally, I was now convinced the bear would be returning for a second visit. Like they do in every story you hear about when a person is attacked by a bear and decides to sleep with their food even after a bear sniffs their campsite the first time.

Then I discovered it wasn’t just my sleeping bag. My sleeping bag liner and pillow were all covered in mold, too. This was going to be a long first night.

At this point, I wasn’t going to be using any of this gear and all I had to rely on was my sleeping pad and a makeshift pillow made from a stuff sack and anything I could find in my pack to give it some volume. I could only hope that all the clothing layers in my pack would be enough to get me through the night as I layered them on, one-by-one.

And because apparently everything comes in threes, I found a tiny tick on my leg while changing clothes for bed.

I crawled into my tent, listened to coyotes howling in the distance, and tried to settle in with a book. Their howls seemed to get closer as the evening went on. Each sound startled me awake, thinking the bear was returning to take me out.

At this point I was questioning even sticking out this backpacking trip and considering calling it quits by calling for a pickup. It was going to be a tougher few days than I’d anticipated. But, as they say, “Never quit on a bad day.” I’d try to make it through the night and assess things tomorrow.

There were three main reasons. First, my sleeping setup was covered in mold, and although I initially refused to use it, I eventually got cold enough to give in. I ended up wearing practically every layer I had in my pack, including three pairs of socks, before finally pulling the moldy sleeping bag over my feet.

Second, every unfamiliar noise had me convinced a bear was circling my tent.

And third, the ATV riders and country boys in trucks seemed to be going strong until around midnight.

Needless to say, I was ready to get moving at sunrise.

The morning brought some beautiful stretches of trail, although there were plenty of overgrown and thorny sections to navigate. At one point, I heard what I believe was another bear charging onto the trail behind me. I made my way quickly toward the busy traffic of CR 316, where I felt a little more comfortable.

I accidentally walked about 0.4 miles past Store 88 where I planned to charge my phone which I needed for navigation and had to backtrack. While there, I met a 70-year-old British guy named Calvin Kline, who was working on fixing up the old place alongside his elderly dog. We chatted for about 45 minutes about life experiences and places we have traveled that we both had in common. One of those unexpected trail encounters that makes long-distance hiking so interesting.

After lunch, I pushed on for another five or so miles until reaching the Salt Springs blue-blaze junction. There was a bench where I’d planned to take my dinner break, but instead I discovered something much more important: a campground another 6.5 miles ahead that had bear boxes.

It was already a little after 5 p.m., but I knew I needed to make it there. I pushed through the remaining miles and arrived shortly after 8 p.m. and hiking by headlamp.

I set up camp, secured my food in the bear box, and finally felt like I could relax a little. Dinner was cold-soaked ramen that I’d started preparing 6.4 miles earlier.

After dinner I tried to access the food in the bear box and the doors were jammed. Great. Now I would really need to pull the plug and call for a pickup in the morning. No food means no fuel to keep hiking, unless I could find someone camping in the area that could help me get the doors unjammed. Eventually I broke into the box and was relieved that I didn’t have to quit, again.

There were other campers around, a secure place to store my food, and a much better chance of getting some sleep.

After the previous night, it felt like a luxury to not have to sleep with my food in this heavily bear dense area.

I woke up at sunrise and headed out through a beautiful prairie section before entering one of my favorite stretches of the entire trip: the Juniper Wilderness Area.

The trail through the forest was absolutely gorgeous. It was one of those sections that makes you forget about all the little inconveniences of backpacking and reminds you exactly why you spend so much time out here.

Eventually, I made my way to Juniper Springs Recreation Area, where I had planned a seven-mile kayak float. The current was ripping pretty good and with all the down trees it made for quite the obstacle course. At one point I was pinned in between a down log and some overhanging brush and ended up snapping my sunglasses into two pieces.

A few miles into the float I met Bryan, who works for the local kayaking company. We ended up floating about 3.5 miles together, chatting and swapping stories about Florida and it’s wild backcountry along the way. It was a nice change of pace from the solitude of the trail.

I camped at the recreation area that evening for $50, charged my electronics, and met a couple from Ohio who work for the North Country Trail. We spent a while chatting and they were eager to ask questions about my experience on The Florida Trail so far as they were day hiking sections of it during their visit to the state.

It was a much-needed reset after two eventful days in the woods.

I woke up at sunrise with the goal of hiking the remaining miles to Alexander Springs, where my parents were scheduled to pick me up.

The morning started off well, but somewhere around lunchtime, I managed to make a pretty significant navigation mistake. I sat down on a log to eat, got back on trail, and somehow ended up hiking in the wrong direction, back toward a road I’d already passed.

By the time I realized what I’d done, I’d walked 1.7 miles in the wrong direction. That meant an additional 3.4 miles of bonus hiking for the day.

Exactly what I needed. Plus, the trail had was quite overgrown and I was covered in spiky stickers.

I picked up the pace to make sure I’d still reach my parents on time. Along the way, I continued seeing plenty of bear scat, including some that looked particularly fresh.

Then I came upon a very large black bear directly on the trail.

I startled it, and it took off running with such incredible speed and force that, for a split second, I was terrified it was charging straight toward me. Thankfully, it veered into the woods and disappeared.

I spent the next mile or so periodically shouting, “HEY BEAR!” with my bear spray close at hand.

For the remainder of the hike, I found myself constantly scanning every turn in the trail, anticipating another bear around the next corner.

It was an interesting balancing act. I needed to speed hike to make my scheduled pickup time, but I also didn’t want to move so quickly as to startle another bear.

Eventually, I made it to the forest road and found a log to sit on while waiting for my parents.

I was exhausted, but incredibly proud of myself.

I had navigated the trail, dealt with unexpected challenges, made mistakes and figured them out, and pushed through situations that would have been much easier with someone else there to lean on.

And honestly? I already felt ready to keep going.

But those miles would have to wait. I couldn’t stand the thought of spending another night in my moldy sleeping bag, especially without a bear canister or bear box to store my food.

One of the things I appreciated most about this trip was how it changed my perspective on Florida.

For a long time, I associated Florida with bustling cities, traffic, and endless stretches of concrete. I spent time commuting an hour to work in Miami, and my idea of escaping the city was taking a scenic backroad on a weekend drive to my home in Fort Lauderdale.

I never really appreciated just how much wilderness existed beyond the interstates connecting Florida’s major cities.

After walking more than 500 miles through Florida’s wilderness over the last several years, I’ve come to see the state in an entirely different light. There are enormous stretches of forests, springs, prairies, rivers, and protected wilderness that feel worlds away from the metropolitan areas most people associate with Florida.

There’s still a wild Florida out there. You just have to get off the interstate to find it.

More than anything, this trip gave me a new appreciation for what I’m capable of on my own.

I’ve spent so much of my backpacking experience alongside Lane, and while I’ve learned an incredible amount from him, I think there’s something important about stepping away from the comfort of having someone more experienced beside you.

You have to trust your own judgment. You have to make your own decisions. When something goes wrong, there’s nobody to immediately turn to for reassurance or a solution.

I loved the solitude. I loved making my own decisions, moving at my own pace, and having the freedom to experience the wilderness on my terms.

And perhaps most importantly, I came away with a confidence that I hadn’t realized I was missing.

I don’t need to wait for someone else to be available to go backpacking. I don’t need someone else’s experience to validate my own abilities.

And I have a feeling this won’t be my last solo adventure.

#8324. High Winds Thwart Latest Everest Attempt

The Russian team has returned to Everest, aiming to reach at least 7,500m, but high winds have again dashed their plans.

The three-man team of Andrei Vasiliev, Sergey Kondrashkin, and Vitaly Shipilov set off yesterday and reached their cached tent at 5,600m. As leader Vasiliev explained, they expected strong winds at summit altitude until Wednesday, but they intended to keep themselves in lower areas, where the wind speed was acceptable.

However, the wind was too strong to go higher than 5,600m today, so they decided to stay put. MountainClub.com, which has access to the team’s InReach tracker, has posted a partial view of the climbers’ current location:

We asked Jost Kobusch of Germany (also planning to climb the West Ridge of Everest this winter) about that location. He confirmed that they are midway up the vertical mixed section leading from the Khumbu Glacier to the Lho La Pass.

This is the expedition’s fourth foray up the mountain. According to Vasiliev, it is also their last chance to acclimatize before a potential summit push. The Russians’ climbing permit is reportedly valid until December 15.

Their future progress will depend on the wind. Multi-model forecasts indicate that winds are expected to decrease on Thursday but not to disappear. The chart by High Asia Avalanche Watch, which compares seven different weather models, predicts that winds will not drop below 45kph at the summit (on Thursday and Friday). They will then pick up again.

Wind speed at the summit of Everest over the next two weeks, by High Asia Avalanche Watch.
