#8321. Te Araroa day 32: A cruisy start to the CSQ, and LOFI is born

20km, Paeroa Rail Trail Motel to Daly’s Clearing hut

We knew we only had a relatively short walk on this first day, and had a fairly relaxed start. We had to walk through Paeroa and grabbed coffee on the way to the famous L&P bottle. For those not in the know, Lemon & Paeroa (L&P) is a lemonade drink ‘world famous in New Zealand,’ as the strapline goes.

Pre CSQ selfie, leaving the motel. By Sinéad, of course!

Me and Sinéad at the L&P bottle. I have funky new socks! Photo by Lindsay

After that, we joined the Hauraki Rail Trail, a cycle path that would take us to the start of the Kaimai mountain range. The bike path was flat and easy walking, and ran next to the road to start with. It was so nice to not have to worry about the cars whizzing past! After a bit the track turned off the road and onto some farmland, and was quite scenic. Annabel was on the phone, but the rest of us walked along mostly together, having some nice chats.

After a bit more farmland, we started following the Ohinemuri River as it headed into Karagahake Gorge. The river was super pretty, but soon we crossed a suspension bridge – the first of several on this trip – and turned onto another path that would lead up a tributary of the main river. I hadn’t realised but this track went through some old mining tunnels, some of which were quite long and dark! Of course we all had head torches though.

Looking up the river towards Karagahake Gorge

Walking through the historic buildings by the river. Photo by Sinéad

On the Windows Walk – view from an old mining tunnel

I guess this is one of the windows they’re talking about

Out the end of the tunnels, the track continued along the river. It was beautiful, easy walking and a great way to ease back into hiking after several days off. I was already glad we came on this side quest! The river was deep and clear and looked amazing to swim in. We knew we would hit a river-side campsite at Dickey’s Flat at around lunchtime so we planned to have a dip there. But at around 11.30 we rounded a corner and saw a beautiful little waterfall with a big pool of water in front of it. It looked too inviting and we decided to swim there and take an early lunch.

Walking along the river. Photo by Annabel

Me and Sinéad getting in the water. Photo by Annabel

The water was freezing! But it was very refreshing. We sat on the river bank to eat lunch and dry off. A large group of people came along to have a tea break there – they looked like a local tramping club and they were doing a loop along a different track back to Karangahake Gorge.

From the waterfall, the track continued along the pretty river to Dickey’s Flat campsite. The river there was also nice, but not as deep or swimmable and we were glad we stopped for an early lunch. At the end of the Windows Walk through the tunnels, the DOC sign had said 4km and 2 hours to the campsite. We scoffed at that at the time, as the path was flat and easy. But after our extended lunch and swim break, it actually did take two hours. No worries, we had plenty of time that day. As we left the campsite, another sign said 3 hours to do the 8km to the hut. Again, we didn’t think it would be that long.

But as we were leaving the car park, the track took us through a field where a just-born calf was trying to stand up for the first time! We stood and watched for quite some time. There was another cow and slightly older calf in the field with them, and they were super cute too! The cows were of a type that I don’t think I’ve seen before. They looked really fluffy and the adults had a very sweet little topknot on top of their heads.

Crossing the river, in classic thru-hiker style with my towel and underwear drying on my pack. Photo by Sinéad

Leaving the cows, the track became a little rougher as it followed the river. I had stuck with the others earlier in the day, but on this slightly more challenging terrain I preferred to move a little faster and pulled ahead a bit. We met up again though when I stopped for water at an accessible bit of river. Shortly afterwards, the track headed up a pretty steep hill which was a shock to the system after 3 days of no hiking and an easy morning!

Clearly the four of us have been hiking together long enough now to have developed a bit of a hive mind. When I caught up to Sinéad and Lindsay after getting water, they said they had been talking about trail names, which I had also been thinking about. Lindsay suggested LOFI for me – last out, first in – for my habit of being the last to leave in the morning and overtaking everyone else partway through the day. I like this, and I think I’ll adopt it. It’s better than Pee Sticks anyway! Annabel we thought should be Gourmet. Her food is always the fanciest trail food you ever did see. Some evidence:

“I’ll be right there, I’m just making a bruschetta right now” – Annabel

“Who bought sourdough? Oh it must be Annabel” – Lindsay

Brought an avocado, pesto, cherry tomato and sundried tomato sandwich on sourdough for lunch this day

Sinéad we agreed should be something to do with swimming. She’s such a water baby and is always the first to suggest a dip! Is there an water nymph in Irish folklore? This is a work in progress.

Lindsay we were struggling with. ‘Is it because I don’t have a distinct personality?’ No Lindsay, you are an individual and we love you very much. But she hasn’t had quite such a recurring theme throughout the hike as the rest of us. Another work in progress!

There was a bit more up and down through some pleasant forest. The bush over here is beautiful, but unfortunately I have seen it quite a lot and I don’t really appreciate it as much as I should. I’m more of a big mountain views girl! Eventually I arrived at the junction for the hut. The sign said 20 minutes but I popped out in the clearing pretty soon after. The hut looked unoccupied, and a quick peek inside confirmed I was the only one around so far. By the time the others were trickling in, I had filtered water and was waiting for my electrolytes to dissolve.

Clearly, I have low standards for hut cleanliness and smell because Lindsay came in and immediately opened all the windows and doors as apparently it smelled damp. I hadn’t noticed up to that point, but she was right. I had been to this hut before, and remembered that there was a fair bit of rubbish around. This was still the case, but overall the hut is in decent condition if a little tired. But it’s always a delight not to have to pitch a tent!

We made dinner, some of us with more success than others… Then Annabel was very keen that we should play a game. Someone had left Snakes and Ladders in the hut, unfortunately without a dice to use. The numbers 1-6 were written inside the lid of the box, and we ‘rolled’ by putting a Connect 4 piece inside and shaking it. After that, we were pretty tired and wanted to go to bed, but I needed to set out the route options for tomorrow. Basically, we could take an easier and more scenic, but longer route, or a shorter but muddier and less nice route. After a bit of discussion, we settled on the longer, scenic route. I thought the two might take around the same time, and sometimes that’s more important than distance. Then we finally called it a night, although twice when I was juuuust falling asleep I was rudely awoken by one of the others hearing scuttling animal sounds. So I put my earplugs in, and went to sleep.

Someone may have overfilled her cooking pot…

Annabel eagerly checks what she has ‘rolled’. Photo by Sinéad

The route briefing. Huts usually have helpful maps in them somewhere! Photo by Annabel

#8318. German Women Climb New Route on Sharphu VI

Last month, five women with the German Alpine Club established a new route on the northwest ridge of Sharphu VI in eastern Nepal. It was only the second overall ascent of the 6,076m peak near Kangchenjunga.

In October, Steffi Feistl, Anna Gomeringer, Kristin Hinkelmann, Kathi Huber, and Fenja Kochl set up their base camp at 4,000m. A huge amount of snow had fallen earlier that season, guaranteeing arduous slogging in some areas.

Their preliminary plan had been to attempt either Sharphu II or Sharphu VI, but Sharphu II’s condition looked too dangerous due to unstable rock, threatening seracs, and hazardous snow conditions.

Sharphu II and VI. Photo: Xtreme Climbers/labels by Gunter Seyfferth

On the other hand, the northwest ridge of Sharphu VI seemed feasible. The team acclimatized over several reconnaissance trips, overnighting up to 4,800m. They then set up their advanced base camp on a moraine ridge at that altitude. Then Kochl, Hinkelmann, and Huber set off over initially easy but deep snow-covered terrain.

They eventually reached a steep section at around 5,300m where powder snow overlying bare rock made placing protection difficult. “The mixed pitches had looked easy, but were steeper than expected,” recalled Huber. “Nasty, granular snow, and no hold on the rock underneath.”

Their work complete, the trio rappelled down, and the following day, Feistl and Gomeringer took their turn. They inched up a difficult mixed pitch followed by 200 vertical meters of burrowing through waist-deep powder.

The route up the northwest ridge of Sharphu VI. Photo: German Alpine Club

After a rest day, the five women set off for the summit. They reached a glacier plateau via a 5,800m, previously unclimbed sub-peak. Here, they bivvied. On October 21, they began the final two kilometers to the main summit. The recent sun had hardened the snow, so they sank at most knee-deep. Eventually, they reached the summit ridge. They had to take turns standing on the summit, because that final ridge was so narrow.

Gomeringer and Kochl on the summit of Sharphu VI. Photo: German Alpine Club

Sharphu VI was first climbed on March 25, 2025, by a Chilean-Nepalese team who thought they’d climbed a different mountain. They went up via the east flank. Before that, Sharphu VI had been attempted only once, in 2023.

The German women’s route featured 1,300m of elevation gain, graded M5, 55°. The expedition was the culmination of the German Alpine Club’s three-year women’s training program.

#8314. Piolet d'Or Climber Bags New Route on Kangchung Shar

Hiroyoshi Manome of Japan and his partners, Koji Shiogai and Subaru Takeda, are back in base camp after climbing a new route via the southwest pillar on Kangchung Shar in the Everest region.

The three climbed the line in four days and three nights from their base in Gokyo, Manome’s home team told ExplorersWeb. They summited in good weather and clear skies yesterday at noon. “The route was particularly interesting, with substantial technical rock climbing,” they explained.

The team believes it is the first ascent of this particular line and, as far as we know, they are right. The Himalayan Database has no record of any previous ascent of the southwest pillar.

Manome during the climb. Photo: Subaru Takeda

Kangchung Shar, located in the Gokyo Valley, has an altitude that varies between 6,030m to 6,103m, depending on the source. The Japanese team has shown that the peak still has plenty of adventurous terrain.

Manome explained before departure that their primary goal was the formidable 1,000m mixed north face, which has been climbed only once, with the east ridge as a backup.

“It will be a technical climb, which suits me just right, and there is little information available, so I think it will be an adventurous climb,” he said. The climber illustrated his plans with the hard-drawn sketch below. However, in the end, the climbers found a third option.

The Japanese team’s two potential routes. Photo: Hiroyoshi Manome

Kangchung Shar was first climbed in 1984 by Franci Knez of Slovenia, on a solo up the northwest ridge from Kangchung La. The 1,000m north face of Kangchung Shar was first climbed by  Zdenek Hak and Jaroslaw Bansky of the Czech Republic on their third try in 2021. No one has repeated it. After summiting, the Czech pair traversed to the south side for their descent.

Another Japanese team climbed neighboring Kangchung Nup (6,090m) in the spring of 2022. The American Alpine Journal describes Kangchung Shar and Kangshung Nup as “a bit like two Matterhorns side by side but two kilometers higher.”

An alpinist for 30 years, Hiroyoshi Manome focuses on technical, alpine-style climbs of 6,000m Himalayan peaks. He received a Piolet d’Or for the first ascent of the 2,200m south pillar of Kyashar (6,770m) in Nepal, with Tatsuya Aoki and Yasuhiro Hanatani. His latest big climb was another first ascent in November 2024, this time of the northeast ridge of Nepal’s Chhopa Bamare (6,109m), with Akitugu Konishi and Kotaro Kunimune.

Hiroyoshi Manome. Photo: The North Face Japan

#8312. The Foothills Trail – Day 2

My alarm went off at 6 a.m. After hitting the snooze button a few times, I was up and packing by 6:30. With my pack loaded up, I was back on trail, passing a large group of overnighters and a couple of fellow FHT thru-hikers. The first half of the day was beautiful, skirting the river and allowing plenty of opportunities to refill my water. I found a spot to relax on some rocks that stretched out over the river. Listening to the current rush downstream like white noise, I started to drift off into what felt like a meditative state. I could have easily fallen asleep right there, but my itinerary was set and I had miles to hike. A quick break from the weight of my pack and a few handfuls of SunChips reenergized me for the remainder of the day, or so I thought.

The second half of my day was rough, as that was where most of the climbing happened. Did my husband fail to mention how many stairs were on this trail? Yes. Did he laugh when I texted him in all caps, “STAIRS!?!” Yeah, he told me he thought it was only right that I find out the stair situation the same way he did, a rite of passage to this trail if you will.

Reaching the top of one climb, I saw a large group of hikers taking a break overlooking Whiteside Mountain. An older gentleman and I made eye contact and exchanged smiles before he quickly turned to the group and yelled, “Hiker!” At that moment, I smirked, playing out a scene in my head: “Step aside for hiker royalty! We’re not worthy! We’re not worthy! Party on, hiker!” Channeling my inner Garth and Wayne from Wayne’s World, I grinned at the group as I passed. They were completely unaware of the daydream keeping me entertained on the trail. Hiking completely solo so far, my inner dialogue was like a hamster on a wheel. I pushed on, eager to get to camp, knowing it was going to be an even colder night.

Stepping out to Fish Hatchery Road Access, I peered up the beautifully paved flat road and then back toward the trail, where a small sign read, “Table Rock St Park 55.9.” It felt like I hadn’t made a dent in the miles. A quick glance at my FarOut app showed three more miles to camp. A gloomy sky sat above me all day, the kind of heavy gray overcast that makes you feel cold just looking at it. My fingers were starting to go numb from the windchill. Wearing only shorts and my long-sleeve sun shirt, I thought about throwing on my rain pants for an extra layer. My husband’s voice echoed in my head, “It’s only cold if you think about it. Three miles, walk fast.” I pushed through and reached camp an hour later.

Walking down into the campsite, I found a roomy spot just off the trail, complete with fire rings scattered throughout and water access tucked behind some bushes. A few widow makers loomed overhead, so I found a spot of least resistance to quickly set up my tent. Everything was damp, as it was every day, and the air was cold, so I decided to build a fire. Most of the wood was damp, but I was eager for warmth since the high for the day was 55°F with a projected low of 33°F.

While dinner rehydrated, I stacked firewood next to the ring and set out to get a small fire going, which happened eventually. Dinner followed, some Mountain House meal with vegetables, possibly a stir-fry? My appetite had been nonexistent since the day before. Still, I forced myself to eat just to give my body what it needed. Sitting by the fire for a while, I hoped to see other hikers, though having just missed the peak FHT season, I wasn’t expecting anyone. Finally, I hung my bear bag, brushed my teeth, and snuggled into my tent for the night. You could hear the occasional car pass by from Route 170. I watched a couple of shows on my phone and closed my eyes, ready to start another day tomorrow.

My initial plan had been to take a week off in December for this trail, but I was worried I’d be miserable on my first solo hike and wanted to make it as good an experience as possible to focus on my gear. Instead, I got the opposite of what I planned for, which summed up exactly what thru-hiking was: unplanned events, constant changes of plans, and unexpected weather. Almost immediately after I finished my hike, daytime temps jumped back into the 60s and nighttime temps into the 40s, the exact weather I had originally hoped for.

#8310. November: A Dangerous Time of Year in the Mountains

A glut of early-winter mountain accidents around the world suggests that this transition season may be the most dangerous time of year. It’s not too cold, and many places don’t have enough snow to impede hiking. It’s tempting to let our guard down.

Just north of Los Angeles this week, an experienced hiker and trail runner died when he slipped on an icy slope while trying to help his son.

Guillermo Batres, 44, was hiking on 2,865m Mount Baden-Powell in California’s San Gabriel Mountains with his 14-year-old son, Sebastian. Sebastian slipped on the icy trail but managed to grab a tree. Batres rushed to help him but slipped himself, falling 150m down a ravine.

Batres, in green, and his son seconds before the fatal slip. Photo: Screenshot

Two passing hikers gave the teen microspikes and helped him to safety. A sheriff’s helicopter lowered a paramedic into the ravine, but Batres was already dead.

Also in California, in Angeles National Forest, Nathan Sakaue, 14, died after falling 150m into an icy ravine. A second teenager also fell but survived with injuries. A third member of the party remained above and summoned help.

Search and Rescue services in the Angeles National Forest have responded to six incidents over the last seven days.

Angeles National Forest, California. Photo: Shutterstock

Elsewhere, a 31-year-old man from the Denver area reached the summit of Colorado’s Humboldt Peak (4,288m) on Sunday morning before suffering a fatal fall.

Winter conditions hampered the search, which lasted two days. Colorado Army National Guard personnel located his body yesterday afternoon.

In Banff National Park, Canada, two skaters fell through thin ice at Lake Louise and were able to clamber out, while a day later, a third skater fell through and died of hypothermia. Skating on “wild ice” is a popular sport in the Canadian Rockies at this time of year, but temperatures fluctuate day to day, and ice that is solid enough today may quickly thin within hours if temperatures rise above freezing.

Early-season skating on Lake Louise in Banff National Park can be magical, as long as the ice is thick enough. Photo: Jerry Kobalenko

In France, a 22-year-old solo hiker was found dead beneath snow following a 24-hour search by Chamonix mountain gendarmes.

Following recent heavy snowfall, avalanche danger in the Mont Blanc massif reached Level 4 out of 5 above 2,200m. Authorities had urged people to reconsider mountain outings, but whether an avalanche caused his death has not been established.

Also in France this week, three separate parties needed rescue when wintry weather set in. On Mont Valier in the Pyrenees, three trail runners poorly equipped for snow needed helicopter evacuation. Elsewhere in the Pyrenees, two inexperienced hikers became stranded in snow and needed a helicopter rescue. And in Isère in the French Alps, four young hikers struggled to descend in deteriorating weather and snow. Rescuers accompanied them to safety.

Italy’s Apennine Mountains. Photo: Shutterstock

A 56-year-old man slipped on snow at around 2,500m between Corno Grande and Corno Piccolo in the Apennine Mountains of central Italy. He suffered serious injuries. His wife administered first aid and called rescuers. As darkness descended, an Italian Air Force helicopter capable of night operations was brought in and eventually airlifted the man to a hospital.

Finally, in Japan’s Ōmine Mountains southeast of Osaka, a mountaineer in his 40s became lost and stranded in the snow and needed rescue.

Accidents happen in mountains throughout the year, but late November is particularly perilous. At times it can feel almost summery, and then without warning, winter hits.

#8306. Sick, Tired Climbers Bail on Everest

At last word, the Russian team attempting Everest’s West Ridge was waiting out high winds in their tent at 5,600m. Twenty-four hours later, the team has revealed their expedition is over.

“We’re back at the lodge; we just don’t have the strength left,” leader Andrei Vasiliev told MountainClub today from Lobuche. He explained that the entire team was suffering from colds and coughs that had accompanied them on their previous trips up the mountain. In addition, Vitaly Shipilov has an injured shoulder.

“We might have been able to push through this current outing, but we objectively wouldn’t have enough left for another push,” Vasiliev went on.

This most recent push was the last acclimatization round the team needed before considering a final summit climb. They intended to reach 7,500m and then rest before the final effort. However, the climbers are exhausted and ill, and the conditions on the mountain are no better. Vasiliev noted the seracs are falling more frequently than they were at the start.

“We’ve decided not to take any unnecessary risks,” he explained.

The team will now focus on a new attempt next spring. “I’m channeling my frustration and dissatisfaction as fuel for a future attempt,” he concluded.

#8303. Revisiting Mount Tyree, Antarctica's Forgotten Peak

In April 2022, we did a story on Mount Tyree, Antarctica’s second-highest mountain. Considering that 566 have attempted Mount Vinson since then, and no one has even tried Tyree, we wanted to revisit this forgotten peak. Why does no one go there anymore? What makes it so hard?

At 4,852m, Tyree is just 40m lower than Vinson. Both lie in the Sentinel Range of the Ellsworth Mountains, approximately 13km apart. Like Vinson, you access the mountain by means of a six-hour flight to Union Glacier Camp in Antarctica, followed by a 200km flight on a ski plane to the base of the mountain.

Mount Tyree from near the summit of Mount Gardner, with the 1967 northwest ridge route facing the camera. In profile on the right is the upper west face, scene of the 1989 Mugs Stump solo. Photo: Damien Gildea

The Grand Couloir has become the closest thing Tyree has to a normal route.

The original route was climbed on January 6, 1967, by Barry Corbet and John Evans during the American Antarctic Mountaineering Expedition.

Their approach involved climbing neighboring Mount Gardner and, using fixed ropes, descending toward the col separating the two mountains.

In 2008, experienced Antarctic mountaineer Damien Gildea, Walter Laserer, and Christian Stangl attempted to repeat the route. They encountered temperatures below -40°C and ultimately concluded that the ridge was too long and complicated to climb and reverse safely in a continuous push. They abandoned the attempt.

Gildea’s firsthand account in the American Alpine Journal illustrates the mountain’s seriousness.

On the lower part of the east ridge of Mount Tyree, beside the east couloir. Photo: Damien Gildea

In November 1989, Mugs Stump made the second ascent of Tyree, 22 years after the first. He climbed a new route involving approximately 2,500m of steep rock and ice:

Writing in the 1999 American Alpine Journal, Gildea assessed Stump’s solo ascents of Tyree and neighboring Mount Gardner as arguably the hardest and biggest climbs accomplished in Antarctica up to that time.

French military climbers Antoine de Choudens and Antoine Cayrol established this route in November 1997. Conrad Anker and Alex Lowe repeated it on December 16 of the same year.

Anker’s account describes approximately 2,400m of climbing on snow, ice, and sections of rock.

Interestingly, in the same American Alpine Journal report, Anker described Vinson’s normal route as “basically an intermediate ski run.”

This, from someone who climbed both mountains in the same Antarctic season.

Two subsequent expeditions demonstrate how much conditions can affect the technical difficulty.

The 2017 team reported sustained front-pointing on hard ice, both in the couloir and on the traverse leading up to it. Their descent alone took 12 hours.

In December 2010, Stangl had attempted the same route but was forced to retreat high on the mountain after his partner was injured by rockfall.

These are very different challenges from ascending Vinson’s fixed ropes.

Only 25 people have summited Tyree by January 2026, and none since 2022. By comparison, almost 150 climbers try Vinson every year. Since 2021-22, there have been 741 Vinson attempts. Most are successful.

In 2017, Pachi Ibarra became the first woman to summit Tyree. Its most recent ascent was on January 1, 2022, by Jennifer Drummond and her four guides. Drummond was collecting the Second Seven Summits at the time, and became the second woman and first U.S. woman to summit Tyree.

As KrisAnnapurna pointed out in her original story on Mount Tyree, its 2,000m+ south face remains unclimbed and is one of the largest walls in Antarctica.

The huge, unclimbed south face of Mount Tyree is one of the greatest unclimbed objectives on the continent. Photo: Damien Gildea

#8299. Barry Blanchard on His Many Lives, and the Tension Between Climbing and Family

Over five decades, Canadian alpinist Barry Blanchard has witnessed the evolution of climbing, summited major peaks around the world, and nearly died a few times –- not always in the mountains. We caught up with the 67-year-old Canadian climber at the Banff Centre Mountain Film and Book Festival, where he presented his new memoir, The Echo: Stories from the Edge of Survival.

In the book, Blanchard avoids no topics or details about climbing, success, and failure, the struggle to combine adventure and family life, and how he has used up his nine lives.

Barry Blanchard speaks to ExplorersWeb’s Angela Benavides. Photo: Jerry Kobalenko

His latest comeback took place after he suffered a traumatic brain injury when he fell down a concrete stairway. “I had 11 skull fractures, and we didn’t know if I would ever be able to guide again or even climb or walk again, so [just in case,] my wife set me up to run a bed-and-breakfast,” he told Explorersweb.

ExWeb: How are you feeling now? Are you totally recovered?

Barry Blanchard: Yeah, the new normal is great. Yeah, you know, about half the people with brain injuries [similar to what I had] don’t survive, so I have nothing to complain about.

I’ve lost a bit of the executive function, basically, the ability to hold three concepts in my mind at the same time. So I’m below Canadian standards with that, but on the other levels of the pyramid, I’m above Canadian standards.

We’re sure it’s been a long, painful process. What were the main challenges during the recovery period? You lost your memory for a while, didn’t you?

Yeah, I had no memory for 13 days; it’s all gone, and I doubt it will ever come back. Now I feel I’ve been cursed with a long memory for long-term events, which was really good for my writing, but my short-term memory during that time was a real challenge.

On top of that is the emotional challenge. As my wife and my daughters pointed out, I was really good at acting like I was okay and talking to people as if I was okay, but they knew I wasn’t okay. It took time, effort, and lots of professional help to recognize and explain to my loved ones how I couldn’t cope with much, that I was not prepared to do what they wanted me to. I learned to say: “I have to finish this thing and then I will move on to the thing you want me to do. But I can’t do it right at the moment.”

How about your balance? As a climber and a guide, that’s pretty vital.

My doctor told me that balance would take the longest to return, and it was true. Initially, I started back in the climbing gym, always on top rope. But soon after going to the climbing gym, I started to go outside. The first thing I did was ice climbing — luckily, with some of the best ice climbers in the world belaying me from above.

Barry Blanchard climbing in the Canadian Rockies in 2022. Photo: Courtesy of Barry Blanchard

On one of the early climbs, I nearly fell over [due to poor] balance. I talked to the people at the hospital, and they pointed out that the brain is 2% of the body mass but it needs 20% of the oxygen. So they gave me a great tip: to stop and breathe. When I feel I am losing balance, I stop and focus on deep breathing for five or 10 minutes. It works.

Also, for a couple of years, the moment I touched the rock, I’d get vertigo, so I just learned to wait for 30 seconds or so till the vertigo passed, and then I could climb. Now that’s gone.

Overall, It’s been an interesting voyage, but I can’t recommend it. Do not get a traumatic brain injury. I don’t know if you have had one, but don’t.

What a twist of fate, after decades engaged in objectively risky climbs, that your closest call was a domestic accident…Do you often reflect on that?

I identified this a long time ago: It’s great to be good at what you do, but you also need luck. The accidents I’ve had in the mountains, I’ve had enough good luck that things worked out. But just adding a little bit of bad luck to those situations, I wouldn’t be here, such as on Howse Peak* in 1999, as I was about to turn 40. If I’d have been six inches farther exposed to the avalanche, I wouldn’t be here.

But you know, there’s some skill involved in that, and my buddy put a good anchor under a little bulge of limestone. The ice screw got ripped out in the avalanche, but the piton held. I was lucky.

The east face of Howse Peak in 1999. Photo by Blanchard’s climbing partner, Steve House

[Note: Howse Peak*, located in Banff National Park, is also the peak where David Lama, Jess Roskelley, and Hansjorg Auer lost their lives in an avalanche in 2019. According to Blanchard, the accident was bad luck.]

In your new memoir, you are extremely honest about your struggle to combine your climbing and personal life. How hard is to be an alpinist and a family man?

I divide my life into four quarters, as in Canadian football. In my first two quarters, almost all was about my passion for alpinism and my belief in it unconditionally. It was my church. In that time, my first marriage ended, and I got a divorce largely because of the tension between alpinism and being a husband, and also not being a loyal husband.

As I explain in the book, my wedding ring was on one hand, and my ice axe was in the other, and I was being kind of pulled apart. My second marriage has also ended, but it gifted me the birth of my two daughters. I was also at the most effective point of my life as an alpinist around 33 to 35.

Then, some things start to change within the body. My reflexes slowed down, and so did my ability to adapt to high altitude. As testosterone decreased, the responsibility of fatherhood increased. Having a daughter changed my point of view about risk and risk tolerance.

Soon after she was born, I was in the Coast Range with my climbing partner from Colorado, Mark Wilford, doing a route on the north face of Bravo Peak. I couldn’t tell whether the snow would stick to 50-55º steep slopes, because it was a maritime snowpack, which is different from the continental snowpack we were used to climbing on at home. [In the Canadian Rockies,] you just don’t get snow sticking like that. Every time we moved a foot or a hand climbing up that type of snow, we were making a judgment about avalanche risk. Every time I made those decisions, I saw Rosemary’s face. It really changed my risk tolerance quite a bit.

Blanchard is back to climbing and guiding. Photo: Courtesy of Barry Blanchard

I heard recently that in the 1970s, Formula 1 drivers won because they were totally prepared to die. And of the 20 Formula One drivers at that time, typically one would die every year. Is that the attitude you have to have going in and how you deal with fear? It’s like, okay, if it happens, it happens, and I’m perfectly okay with it?

In the late ’70s, early ’80s, we used to have a saying among ourselves, kind of joking, but it came true for some of my fellow alpinists: “I’m glad we didn’t die, now we can try something harder.”

Now, being a father is the most important thing for me.

Over decades of climbing around the world, you have seen expeditions evolve from pioneering ascents to the huge commercial expeditions on Everest. From your point of view, what has changed and what remains the same?

The thing that is the same is the experience inside the alpinist, at the heart of the alpinist, and the fear of falling. That fear doesn’t change. And what has changed over time is technology: it’s easier to stay warm, it’s easier to go lighter, we have far better ice tools and ice screws, all that stuff.

We do climb harder now; we climb faster, we climb steeper, thanks to modern training methods. Weather forecasts are so good now, but the heart of an alpinist and the fear remain. In fact, one of the gifts of alpinism is that you learn to make fear an ally. That fear is your body demanding more security. If you allow your fear to progress to panic, you’re going to fall.

Blanchard on Nanga Parbat in 1988. Photo: Courtesy of Barry Blanchard

You are of Métis heritage. How have your indigenous roots shaped your relationship to mountains and nature?

I’m Métis, which is a separately identified culture in Canada. We’re a mixed breed, basically half European, half indigenous. The indigenous side of my bloodstream allows me to look at nature and perceive I am related to everything: the trees, the rocks, the mountain…Everything is alive, nothing is dead, everything has a spirit.

I’ve had some really powerful spirits in my life. In 1980 in Chamonix, after the hardest climb that my buddy Kevin [Doyle] and I did, we were down in our illegal campground in the Chamonix Valley, and I leaned my back against a large tree and wrapped my arms around the sides. Then I felt the ancestor in the tree, and that ancestor told me to dedicate my life to alpinism. It happened right there; that’s when I made the decision. And now, one of my really important ancestors is the mountain that is the namesake of our guiding company. Colonists call it Yamnuska, but the Stony Nakoda people call it Îyâ Mnathka (pronounced Iyamunushka) — which translates to “flat-faced mountain.”

I’ve spent over 500 days of my life on Îyâ Mnathka, who is a very important ancestor for me. In particular, there is one tree that I’ve been touching and standing around and even anchoring off of for over 40 years — and it’s a tough place on top of this mountain to make a living as a tree. When I go to the mountain, I offer tobacco to the land at the base of the mountain and ask for permission. And then when I get to the rock, I touch the rock and take some time to just feel it and communicate with that ancestor before I leave. Sometimes the ancestor is good to me, and sometimes it’s not, like all mountains.

That’s why I hate the word “conquering” applied to heading up on Everest in the conga line. If you get to the top, it’s because that ancestor allows you to get to the top. There’s nothing conquered about it.

You have worked in several mountain-related Hollywood films as a climbing double or safety advisor, including the recent Tenzing film, by Jennifer Peedom. Please tell us about it.

I’m really proud of this one. It’s differently from what I felt after Cliffhanger or Vertical Limit, films in which I also participated. On Tenzing, I was the mountain safety officer. I was actually teaching Willem Dafoe and Tom Hiddleston, who play Hillary, about climbing in 1953 climbing equipment.

Unfortunately, I had to leave the role because my ninth cat life got used up in New Zealand. I lost an edge skiing on a very frozen surface and took a bad fall and suffered a few fractured bones.

In fact, Blanchard has had so many surgeries, replacements, and metal pieces in his body that he considers himself one of the best users of Canada’s public health system.
